title: CGT Calculator Post-2026 Federal Budget
body:
O.P.
I've been seeing a lot of discussion around dealing with the new tax rules for CGT, so I've put together a calculator to help assess the impacts of the new rules and what it means for your investments.
https://capgains.au
Plenty of options for configuration of inputs are available including asset classes, assumed rates, dates of acquisition before/after rule implementation, expected purchase and sale price. Some visualisations to assist with projection of profit and tax liability going forward is also included.
Hope this helps us to have better informed discussions around these changes. Any and all feedback is greatly appreciated.

[User #643904526 postsArgonaut73Achilles Last StandWhirlpool Enthusiast] this post was edited
From 1984 to 2000 you used CPI and after that Howard introduced the 50% discount. I looked at my investments using CPI and came to the conclusion that 25% was about right for assets held a while. My opinion is that Howard made a big mistake and should have gone for 25%. If he did that I doubt we would have the total mash of rules that Labor has just come up with now.
CPI is quite logical, but for shares with dividend reinvestment plans the maths is a nightmare, which is why I gave up on DRPs. Unless you kept a detailed spreadsheet of all shares, when you come to sell, the rule I think is last in first out. So selling part of the portfolio is messy and easy to get wrong. As an example, for an asset bought in 1990 I used CPI to get to a base cost in 2000 and then used the 50% method after that.
25% would be ok in my humble opinion as it is simpler.
Edit – I tried the calculator but it doesn't seem to handle the pre 2000 purchase date using CPI. I guess I could input that myself and say purchase date is 01/01/2000. In my case the CPI was 59.9 when bought and 69.1 in 2000. So $100K base cost is $115,358 on start 2000. Note that CPI figures may vary as the base year quarter, stated as 100, may vary depending on the website you go to. It is ratio of any two quarters that is the same though.

Not so. You can choose which one you wish to sell, probably basing the selection on whether you wish to maximise the loss, minimise the gain, or vice versa.
I also gave up on DRP because of the accounting challenges it created. ,

en312 writes...
Is the ATO going to include a historical inflation table for CGT calculation
They already do. It It will be based on the RBA published rates.
Will this table be year-to-year, month-to-month, day-to-day?
The pre 1999 rules required adjusting the cost of an asset quarterly, The budget did not specify (as far as I’m aware) if the new rules will also be quarterly.
If the ATO updates Jun 30, 2XXXX inflation on Sep 30, XXXX will the tax file due date be moved from Oct 30, 2XXX to Jan 30, 2XXX+1?
The RBA publishes the CPI 4 weeks after quarter end, so you should have it by end of July. It could be the ATO publishes something before the end of June anyway, like using the rate for the previous quarter.
